title: How Much Should an Ensuite Renovation Cost in Winnipeg?
metaTitle: How Much Should an Ensuite Renovation Cost in Winnipeg?
metaDescription: What sets the cost of an ensuite renovation in Winnipeg: layout, shower, plumbing moves and finishes, plus timelines, permits and where to see prices.
excerpt: An ensuite costs what its decisions cost: whether the toilet and shower stay where they are, how big the shower is, how much tile goes on the walls and whether the room grows into a closet. Here is how to think those choices through before you ask for a price.
answer: An ensuite should cost about the same as a full bathroom of the same size and finish level, so start with our [bathroom renovation cost guide](/services/bathroom-renovations/cost) for current Winnipeg price ranges. Where your ensuite lands in that range depends mostly on plumbing moves, the type of shower, how much tile and glass it has, and whether the room is enlarged.

faqs.q: Is an ensuite cheaper to renovate than a main bathroom?
faqs.a: Not on its own. An ensuite and a main bathroom of the same size and finish level cost about the same to renovate. Ensuites often end up costing more because people choose larger showers, double vanities and more tile for a private space. Keeping the existing plumbing layout is the most reliable way to control the price.

faqs.q: Can I turn the tub in my ensuite into a walk-in shower?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Building a walk-in shower where the tub was reuses the existing drain area, which keeps costs down. A curbless shower needs the floor sloped to the drain, which can mean work on the floor framing. We check the floor structure and the drain location during the free on-site visit before quoting it.

faqs.q: How long will my ensuite be out of use?
faqs.a: Plan on two to three weeks of on-site work for a typical bathroom, and longer if plumbing moves, the room is enlarged or custom glass is ordered after the tile is finished. Because an ensuite is rarely the only bathroom in the house, it can usually stay closed off while the work is done.

faqs.q: Should I add a heated floor to my ensuite?
faqs.a: If the budget allows, a renovation is the time to do it, because the floor is already open. Electric floor heating adds materials, a thermostat and electrical work, so it is a modest line item rather than a small one. In a Winnipeg winter it is the difference between a cold tile floor and a comfortable one.

faqs.q: Where can I see current ensuite renovation prices?
faqs.a: Our bathroom renovation cost guide lists the starting ranges our instant estimator uses for bathrooms, by size and option, and an ensuite falls within those ranges. The instant estimate gives a range for your own room, and the free written quote after an on-site visit gives you a price you can sign.

blocks.x: An ensuite is the bathroom attached to a bedroom, usually the main bedroom. Because it is private, people tend to want more from it than from a hall bathroom: a bigger shower, two sinks, better lighting, sometimes a soaker tub. Each of those choices moves the price, and a few of them move it a lot. This guide explains what drives the cost so you can decide where your money does the most.
Where do ensuite renovation prices come from?

Our current price ranges for bathrooms, including ensuites, are in the bathroom cost guide linked above: the starting ranges our own instant estimator uses, not national averages. An ensuite sits in those ranges according to its size and the options you choose. The decisions below decide whether it lands at the lower or higher end of its range.

For a range on your own room, the [instant estimate](/instant-quote) asks a few questions about size and finishes. It is an estimate, not a quote: the price you sign is the free written quote that follows a free on-site visit, once the drains, walls and floor have been looked at.
What changes the cost of an ensuite the most?

Moving plumbing, changing the type of shower and adding tile and glass usually move the price the most. Keeping the toilet, shower drain and vanity where they are is the single biggest saving. Finishes matter too, but layout decisions set the floor of the budget before any tile is chosen, so settle the layout first.

blocks.x: Which ensuite layout works for your space?

The right layout depends on the room's width and where the drains and stack run. A narrow ensuite usually suits fixtures in a single row along one wall, while a wider room can take a separate shower and a double vanity. If the bedroom can spare closet space, a modest expansion often solves more than a more expensive finish would.

blocks.x: How long does an ensuite renovation take?

Most bathrooms we renovate take two to three weeks of on-site work, from demolition to the final bead of caulking. An ensuite with plumbing moves, custom glass or an expansion into the bedroom can take longer, mainly because custom glass is measured after the tile is done and some fixtures and finishes have long lead times.

Because it is not usually the only bathroom in the house, an ensuite is easier to live through than a main bathroom. Plan where you will sleep if dust and noise are next to the bedroom, and choose the vanity, fixtures and tile before demolition so nothing waits on a delivery. You get weekly progress updates while the work is under way.
Do you need a permit for an ensuite renovation in Winnipeg?

Often, yes. The City of Winnipeg lists bathrooms among the home renovations that may need a building permit, and plumbing or electrical work can need separate trade permits. Cosmetic changes such as painting and flooring do not need a building permit. We coordinate the permits and inspections with the City, or with your local municipality outside Winnipeg.
Our guide to [renovation permits in Winnipeg](/blog/winnipeg-renovation-permits) explains which projects need which permits and how the inspections fit into the schedule.
Which ensuite upgrades are worth paying for?

Spend on what you use every day and what is hard to change later: a properly waterproofed shower, ventilation that removes moisture, good light at the mirror and enough storage. Backing in the walls for future grab bars costs little while the walls are open and a lot once the tile is up.
An exhaust fan vented outdoors, not into the attic. Health Canada recommends running a bathroom fan when you shower and for at least 30 minutes afterwards.
Plywood backing behind the walls around the toilet, tub and shower. CMHC notes that it allows grab bars and handrails to be installed later without opening the walls.
Layered lighting: a ceiling fixture for the room and lighting at the mirror for grooming.
A vanity with drawers rather than only doors, so storage is easy to reach and organize.
A heated floor if the budget allows, since it is simplest to add while the floor is open.
